autointerp.description: This neuron fires on the "<start_of_turn>" token that begins the model's reply, right after a math word problem's final question and "<end_of_turn>\n".

The neuron fires on a person's first name that begins a new clause as its subject, usually right after "If" or "when" or at the start of a sentence in a math word problem, where it is about to be followed by a verb or possessive.

This neuron fires on function words or verbs (like "each," "for," "in," "to," "that") in the middle of a math word problem's question or final clause, where the sentence is about to specify the object or quantity being asked about or computed.

This neuron fires on tokens where the model is about to commit to or continue a named entity or answer, such as a person's name after a title or first name (Katy, Mrs. Cruz, Mr. Tan) and the start of a proposed capital-city answer

This neuron fires on function words or punctuation (like "the", "of", "and", or a period/comma) in the middle of a math word problem, usually just after a noun or verb phrase where a continuation like an object or noun phrase is expected.
This neuron fires on function words (especially "is" after "I think the answer") that directly precede a predicted content word or answer, such as a stated answer or a noun phrase.
This neuron fires on the end-of-turn token that closes a short, simple factual question (basic arithmetic or "what comes after X"), right before the model must produce a brief answer.

This neuron fires on a word that sits just before an expected number or continuation in word-problem phrasing, such as "another," "takes," "comes," "get," "also" and "different," and it also fires on the word "hard" in the question "What is the opposite of '

This neuron fires on tokens within a person's first name (often a multi-token or unusual name, or possessive after a name) near the start of a math word problem, where the name is the subject being introduced.

It fires on the head noun or entity word in a math word problem that refers back to a previously mentioned group or item (such as "runner," "rabbits," "rest," or "second") just before a quantity relation or comparison is completed.

This neuron fires on the closing quote-and-question-mark token ("'?") that ends a "What is the opposite of '[word]'?" question, especially when the word is a spatial or directional term like left, above, up, or inside.

This neuron fires on tokens that mark a transition point where the next piece of content is a new event or answer, such as the subject or particle after a temporal connective ("turns around," "came back," "until she," "and then") and the end-of-turn token after a short factual question
The neuron fires on a space (or odd byte-fragment) token that comes right before a number in math word problems, so it appears to predict that a digit comes next.
This neuron fires on the token right before a stated numerical answer to a simple "X plus Y" arithmetic question, mainly on "is" in "the answer is" and on a leading "1" in a user's guessed answer.
The neuron fires on the question mark ending a user's "Which continent is [country] in?" question, at the point where the model is about to answer with the country's continent.

This neuron fires mainly on the word "and" right after a person's first name at the start of a prompt (e.g., "Brittany and her mom"), where a second character is about to be introduced, with weaker activations on other tokens in math word problems.

This neuron fires on the first token or fragment of a person's name (often a split or rare name) or a sentence-initial word, such as "I", that begins a new sentence or clause, especially early in a user's math word problem.

This neuron fires on tokens in math word problems that are early-sentence names (especially female first names like Brittany, Melanie, Sandra, Amy, Isabelle) or the quantity word "one" or "a" that introduces a unit amount.

This neuron fires on function words and possessive markers (especially "the" after prepositions like "of" or "in", and the apostrophe in names like "Fred's") that sit at the start of a phrase and predict an upcoming noun or time/ordinal expression

This neuron fires on possessive pronouns ("his"/"her") that come right after a verb or preposition (e.g. "asks," "from," "of," "with") and refer back to the sentence's subject, usually in a maths word problem.
